kits.familyName: Why original ideas matter at work
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}, where the team is looking for fresh ideas.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are asked to help the team stand out.
detail: It is the middle of the afternoon.
pressure: {coworker3} says it is not worth the trouble.
You are in a hurry to finish.

tiers.1: A good idea starts with a real need that people have.
tiers.2: Originality means building your own version, not copying.
tiers.3: Feedback can reshape an idea instead of ending it.
tiers.4: A small test shows whether an unusual idea works.
tiers.5: Standing out comes from something customers actually notice.

fact: Customers keep asking for something the workplace does not offer, and you have an idea for a small new service.
issues.short: your idea for a new service
issues.action: Write up the idea with the customer requests and give it to {lead|the}.
issues.brief: write up the idea with the requests
issues.reason: Requests from real customers show that the idea answers a need, which makes it easier to take seriously.
issues.lesson: Back an idea with the real need it answers.

shortcut.text: Wait until someone asks you for ideas before you mention it.
shortcut.why: The team cannot use an idea nobody hears, and the customer requests are the strongest part of it.
shortcut.mis: Ideas only count when management asks.

clear: You already gave {lead|the} your service idea along with the customer requests.

fact: A competitor's flyer has a clever layout, and you are designing the workplace's own flyer.
issues.action: Take inspiration from the layout, but design your own for this workplace.
issues.brief: borrow the inspiration and design your own
issues.reason: A copied layout makes your workplace look like the competitor, while your own version shows what is different.
issues.lesson: Learn from good ideas, then build something that is yours.

shortcut.text: Copy the layout exactly, since it already works.
shortcut.why: A copy hides what is different about your workplace and is not original work.
shortcut.mis: If it works for them, copying is the safest choice.

clear: You already designed a flyer of your own that takes inspiration from the competitor's.
issues.done: the flyer design is already your own

fact: {Lead|the} said your idea would not work as described, but added that one part of it could help.
issues.short: the part of your idea that could help
issues.action: Ask which part could help, and reshape the idea around it.
issues.brief: ask which part helps and reshape the idea
issues.reason: An idea that is partly useful is a starting point, and the person who spotted it can help you improve it.
issues.lesson: Use feedback to improve an idea instead of dropping it.

shortcut.text: Drop the idea, since it was turned down.
shortcut.why: One part was called useful, so dropping all of it wastes what could be built on.
shortcut.mis: A turned-down idea has no value.

clear: You already reshaped the idea around the part that {lead|the} liked.

fact: You have an unusual idea for the lobby display, and {lead|the} is open to a small test.
issues.short: the idea for the lobby display
issues.action: Try it in a small test and ask customers what they think.
issues.brief: try a small test and ask customers
issues.reason: A small test shows whether an unusual idea works before the whole display depends on it.
issues.lesson: Test unusual ideas on a small scale and learn from the results.

shortcut.text: Wait until you are sure it will work before trying anything.
shortcut.why: You cannot be sure without trying, and waiting leaves a possibly good idea unused.
shortcut.mis: An idea should be perfect before it is tried.

clear: You already ran a small test of the display idea and collected comments.

fact: The team is asked how to stand out from a nearby competitor that offers a very similar service.
issues.short: the ways to stand out from the competitor
issues.action: Suggest something customers would notice that the competitor does not offer.
issues.reason: Customers choose what they can see is different, so a visible difference does more than a small price change.
issues.lesson: Look for differences that customers can see and value.

shortcut.text: Suggest lowering prices below the competitor's.
shortcut.why: A price cut can be copied quickly, and it does not show what is different about your workplace.
shortcut.mis: The lowest price is the only way to compete.

proceed.text: Carry on with your regular work, since nothing here needs action.
proceed.why: Each of these situations involves how an original idea is found, shaped and tested.
proceed.lesson: Original ideas come from real needs, are built in your own way, improve with feedback and are tested small.

generic.text: Ask {coworker2} what they usually do and copy that.
generic.why: A coworker's habit is not the written guide, and it may be out of date.
generic.mis: Common practice is the same as the rule.

generic.text: Wait until {lead|the} brings it up before you act.
generic.why: The guide applies to you now, and waiting leaves the problem in place.
generic.mis: Someone else will raise it if it matters.

overcaution.text: Refuse to suggest any idea unless it has already been proven to work elsewhere.
overcaution.why: The point is to find new ideas. Waiting for proof elsewhere stops original work.
overcaution.mis: Only proven ideas are worth suggesting.

setup: You have an idea that might improve how the workplace helps customers.

steps.text: Note the customer need behind it
Write a short description of the idea
Run a small test if {lead|the} agrees

rel: The description should explain the need.
process.lesson: Name the need, describe the idea, share it, then test it small.

title: Notes on creative ideas
intro: You are reading a coworker's draft advice on creative ideas at work.
prompt: Which line gives advice that would hurt creativity?
doc.lesson: Creative work starts with needs, builds on feedback and tests ideas small.

lines.text: Start from a need that real customers have.

bad.text: Pick an idea you like and look for customers who want it later.
bad.why: An idea that starts without a real need is harder to use.

lines.text: Learn from good ideas, then build your own version.

bad.text: Copy ideas that work for others so you do not waste time.
bad.why: A copy hides what is different about your workplace.

lines.text: Use feedback to reshape an idea.

bad.text: Drop an idea once someone says it will not work as described.
bad.why: Part of it might help, and feedback can show which part.

lines.text: Test unusual ideas on a small scale first.

review.notes: Everyday creativity only; no product, brand or outside program is named. Tiers: real need, own version, feedback, small test, standing out.
